system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms (for example rates by inhibitor level, dose-normalised concentrations, effect against concentration over time).
3. Retrieve: search the mechanism library and read the relevant cards. They give equations, data signatures, pitfalls and the library model name to fit.
4. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
5. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
6. Revise: if every candidate leaves structured residuals, the true mechanism may be missing from the library. Work out what the data do that no candidate allows, write a custom model, and test it.
7. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
8. Submit with submit_model, citing fit_ids (and card ids you read) as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) (no inhibitor, I = 0). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 16 rows with columns: S, v. Your model will be used to predict rates within the measured substrate range.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

steps: Compare Michaelis-Menten vs substrate inhibition vs Hill models
Check residuals and identifiability, submit best

name: fit_model

content.thinking:
The Michaelis-Menten fit comes out with a huge Vmax and Km, so the curve looks almost linear, with a slope around 0.195. But the measured points don't follow that line: they're low at small S and climb faster than linear, so the data might be sigmoidal at low concentrations before saturating. I want to look at the raw points more closely, starting with v/S.

Scanning the velocity-to-substrate ratios, most points sit near 0.19–0.20, though the first point at S=1 runs high and S=0.5 runs low. That pattern suggests the data is essentially linear with no saturation up to S=20, so I'll fit a linear rate model and also test substrate inhibition using the correct Ksi key.

content.text: The MM fit diverged to Vmax ≈ 990 and Km ≈ 5000, so the data look almost linear in S over this range. I'll check that directly and refit substrate inhibition with the correct parameter names.

name: fit_model
fit_model

content.thinking:
The linear model wins on BIC, and the substrate-inhibition term collapses to linear, so I'm dropping it. Residuals look clean, with no leftover structure, and the duplicate points at S=0.5 don't change that. I'll record the hypotheses and submit linear_rate as a first-order fit, since saturation isn't visible up to 20 µM, which puts Km above that range.

I'm settling the Km question: the Michaelis-Menten fit puts it near 5000, which the data can't really pin down, so all I can say is that Km is well above 20 µM.

content.text: The linear model has the lowest BIC, and the substrate-inhibition and MM fits both collapse onto it. I'll record the hypotheses and submit.

input.mechanism: First-order regime: v = k*S, with S much less than Km over the measured range (Km effectively >> 20 uM)
input.prediction: v/S roughly constant across S; no saturation or inhibition in 0.5-20 uM
input.evidence: fit3: k=0.194 (1% SE), sigma 0.112, BIC -68.3, no residual structure. v/S ~0.19-0.20 for S>=6.
fit1: Vmax and Km diverge (Km ~5000, Vmax/Km fixed); BIC -65.6 worse than linear; no plateau in data.

input.prediction: Rate falls at high S (substrate inhibition) or sigmoidal shape (Hill)
input.evidence: fit4: Ksi -> infinity (no inhibition), fit2 Hill n=0.98 with huge K (reduces to linear); both worse BIC than fit3.

input.summary: Over 0.5-20 uM the rate is proportional to substrate, v = k*S with k = 0.194 uM/min per uM (1% SE). Michaelis-Menten saturation (fit1), substrate inhibition (fit4) and Hill cooperativity (fit2, n~0.98) all converge to this linear limit, with Km effectively much greater than 20 uM and no inhibition, and linear has the lowest BIC (-68.3 vs -65.6 for MM). Residuals show no structure.
nonidentifiable_params: Km (only a lower bound, Km >> 20 uM, is supported)
Vmax (only the ratio Vmax/Km = 0.194 is determined)
